title: Briefing: South Africa, India, France, Serbia, Italy, Canada, Germany and Albania
script: Good morning. It's Wednesday, November fourth, and this is the Unowned briefing: the stories that matter, checked and graded. It's read by a synthetic voice, and every fact comes from our published timelines.
Every item carries our grade. Confirmed means independent outlets agree. Reported means one source so far. Disputed means the accounts conflict. And alleged is one side's claim.
Here are the top stories.
South Africa. Today: South African Government says asylum seekers and refugees cannot vote, citing refugee regulations and Electoral Act.
India. Today: Cockroach Janta Party says on X there could be election rigging in India, not vote theft.
France. Yesterday: Unions list 45 strike calls, keep Rennes march route despite ban, expect larger turnout.
Serbia. On Monday: Serbia's top prosecutor orders action on student complaints; police chief Kričak stays in custody.
Italy. On Monday: Italy union says a strike is the only choice after school budget cuts.
Canada. On Monday: new developments in Canada's Pacific Link pipeline fight.
Germany. On Monday: Education Minister Karin Prien deems youth protests legitimate, pledges dialogue; SPD urges education summit.
Albania. On Monday: Jailed Tirana mayor Erion Veliaj accuses Prime Minister Edi Rama of orchestrating his prison transfer.
Now the details.

South Africa. Today: South African Government said on X that asylum seekers and refugees are not allowed to vote, citing refugee regulations and the Electoral Act. That's the authority's own claim, from its official statement, and we grade it alleged until independent reporting backs it up. Coming up: The new asylum appointment system Home Affairs said would be in place by November tenth.

India. Today: Cockroach Janta Party said on X that there could be election rigging in India, not vote theft. That's their own claim, posted on their channel, and we grade it alleged. Coming up: The Special Executive Magistrate hearing for the CJP leaders summoned over the Jantar Mantar protest listed for the third week of November.

France. Yesterday, Tuesday, November third: Unions have listed 45 specific strike calls across sectors ahead of the November 5 protest in Rennes and say they will keep the march route despite a prefectural ban. Ouest‑France reports the unions expect a larger turnout than the 15,000 demonstrators who marched on October 31. Our grade: reported, from a single source so far. Also yesterday: France: unions say a nationwide strike on November fifth is shaping up to be large, with the CGT counting 1,140 strike notices across its organisations, Ouest-France reports. We grade that reported: so far only Ouest-France has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Turnout and outcome of the unions' November fifth interprofessional strike and demonstration.

Serbia. On Monday, November second: Serbia's Supreme Public Prosecutor's Office orders the Belgrade prosecutors to act on student complaints against criminal police chief Marko Kričak over an August 2025 incident in a Government of Serbia garage, which had gone more than a year without result, Vreme reports. The paper says Kričak, detained on November first, was still in custody on November third. Our grade: reported. It rests on one source, Vreme, and isn't yet confirmed by a second. Coming up: Formation of the new government and the choice of prime minister.

Italy. On Monday, November second: Italy: la Repubblica reports the government's school budget plan would cut about 350 teaching posts in Emilia-Romagna, and the FLC-CGIL union says a strike is "the only choice". The UIL union estimates 70 to 80 fewer posts in Bologna province; the FLC-CGIL also criticises bonuses for private schools. We grade that reported: so far only la Repubblica has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Turnout and outcome of the CGIL general strike called for November twentieth.

Canada. On Monday, November second: Nine British Columbia First Nations announce Federal Court applications to quash the Pacific Link national-interest designation, saying Ottawa did not adequately consult them. Ottawa says it consulted more than 110 Indigenous communities and will offer a minimum 10 per cent ownership stake, The Globe and Mail and the Vancouver Sun report; Cold Lake First Nation filed the first challenge in October. Our grade: confirmed by independent reporting. Coming up: Whether binding Pathways carbon-storage agreements are signed by the November fifteenth target.

Germany. On Monday, November second: Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien calls the concerns of the young people who marched in more than 30 cities on October thirty-first "legitimate and extremely relevant" and promises more dialogue, and SPD politicians call for a national education summit; these are proposals, not policy changes so far, The Local reports. We grade that reported: so far only The Local Germany has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Gen Z regelt plans another countrywide protest on November fourteenth.

Albania. On Monday, November second: Albania's jailed Tirana mayor, Erion Veliaj, accuses Prime Minister Edi Rama of orchestrating his October twenty-eighth prison transfer, which the government denies. Veliaj, held in pre-trial detention on corruption charges he denies, also said Justice Minister Toni Gogu demanded he give up control of the city, Tirana Times reports; the claims, relayed in part by his lawyer, are unverified. Our grade: disputed. The sides tell it differently, and both versions are on the story page.
That's the Unowned briefing for Wednesday, November fourth. Full timelines, and every source, are at unowned news dot com. Thanks for listening.
